one_liner: Header-only C++ fixed-size tensor library whose small-GEMM kernels match MKL JIT and beat padded Blaze.
what_it_does: Fastor provides compile-time-sized tensors (Tensor<double,3,3>, Tensor<float,2,3,5,...>) with NumPy-like views, einsum/permute/contraction, and small dense linear algebra (matmul, det, inv, LU, QR, solve). It is its own API, not a drop-in for Eigen or Blaze, though TensorMap wraps existing C arrays without copying. Lazy expression templates evaluate on assignment or evaluate().
how_it_is_fast: All sizes are template parameters, so SIMD kernels (SSE2 to AVX-512, FMA) for matmul and contractions are statically dispatched and fully unrolled for the exact shape, with no runtime dispatch or heap allocation. 'Smart' expression templates rewrite expressions at compile time (e.g. trace(A^T B) to inner(A,B), det(inv(A)) to 1/det(A), matrix-chain reordering) and a compile-time cost model picks a FLOP-minimal contraction order for tensor networks. Optional LIBXSMM or MKL-JIT backends can take over matmul.
when_to_use: Many repeated small dense ops (roughly 2x2 to 64x64, sizes known at compile time), e.g. per-element or per-quadrature-point kernels in finite-element / continuum mechanics codes.
Higher-order tensor contractions and einsum with fixed dimensions, where compile-time contraction-order optimisation cuts FLOPs.
Embedded / FPGA / no-heap environments: no dynamic allocation and no RTTI.
When you want small-GEMM speed near MKL JIT/LIBXSMM without linking a vendor library.
when_not_to_use: Medium or large matrices: issue #42 reports Fastor ~2x slower than Eigen at 128x128 (fine at 8x8, equal at 64x64); matmul is a register-blocked loop nest without the cache tiling/packing/threading of a BLAS.
Runtime-sized data: there is no dynamic-size tensor type.
Non-x86 SIMD: the built-in SIMDVector layer covers SSE2..AVX-512 only; other architectures fall back to scalar unless you configure the Vc or std::experimental::simd backend.
Large dot products/reductions over long vectors: open issue #141 shows einsum ~2.3x slower than hand-written OpenMP-SIMD/AVX2 at 100k elements (while far faster on small ones).
Projects that need a broad, actively developed library: commits are sparse (two in 2025, two in 2024).

integration.dependencies: none (optional: LIBXSMM, MKL JIT, sleef, Vc)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (config.h #errors below it); tested GCC 5.1-10.1, Clang 3.6-10, ICC 16-19, MSVC 2019
integration.platforms: x86 / x86-64 with SSE2-AVX-512 kernels; other CPUs via scalar fallback or Vc/std::experimental::simd backend
integration.thread_safety: not documented (value-type tensors on the stack; no shared state described)

gotchas: Performance depends on -march/-mavx2 -mfma/-mavx512* flags and -DNDEBUG; without them it compiles to SSE2 or scalar code.
auto on an expression or view holds an unevaluated expression/reference; assign to a Tensor to materialise it.
matmul(A, transpose(B)) creates a temporary transpose (per maintainer in issue #42).
Large fixed sizes live on the stack and inflate compile time and binary size.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Fastor over LIBXSMM when you want a header-only, high-level tensor API (einsum, views, small LU/QR/inverse) for fixed shapes rather than a JIT GEMM library; LIBXSMM is the better choice for runtime-shaped small GEMM or DL primitives. Pick it over TCL when tensor shapes are compile-time and small; TCL targets larger runtime-shaped contractions.
verified_claims_summary: The wiki's small-GEMM benchmarks (cbrt(MNK) <= 128, single-threaded, float/double/complex) against Eigen 3.3.7, Blaze 3.7, LIBXSMM (Apr 2020 devel) and MKL JIT 2021.01, built with GCC 9.2 -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx2 -mfma on i5-8259U and Xeon E3-1240 v6 and GCC 7.4 with AVX-512 flags on Xeon Gold 6128, show Fastor at parity with MKL JIT and padded Blaze roughly 50% slower (up to 2x in some cases). Results are plots only, and the Eigen gap is not quantified in text.
status_note: MIT-licensed, not archived, but low activity (last commits July 2025, previous ones 2024); v0.6.4 is the latest release and the benchmark library versions date from 2020.
